chapters.title: What are we actually building?
chapters.summary: A careful bookkeeper for one very small job.
paragraphs: A bank message says £120 arrived for tenant-a, with the reference “Payment INV-1”. The bookkeeper needs to decide which unpaid invoice that payment settles. This program records the message, checks a suggested match, records a person’s approval and writes the accounting entry.

The £120 has already moved at the bank. This program does not transfer money. An invoice is a bill a customer owes. Reconciliation means connecting the bank payment to the right bill in the business records.

The exercise permits either a local API or a command-line program with a persistent database. This implementation uses Go commands and SQLite, which saves records in a local file. A JSON fixture supplies the suggestion that a model might otherwise produce. There is no real model call, paid API or deployment requirement. VAT, currency conversion, partial payments and split payments are outside the exercise.
A tenant is one organisation using the program. tenant-a and tenant-b may each have an invoice called INV-1. To identify the right bill, the program must use both the organisation and the invoice ID.

The difficult cases begin after the first successful run. The bank may resend its message. A suggestion may pick the wrong bill. Two workers may try to record the same payment. The program may stop after saving an entry but before reporting success. None of these cases should create a second financial entry or bypass approval.

The implementation therefore makes five promises: one financial effect per payment; explicit rules before acting; approval tied to the exact suggestion reviewed; accounting writes that all succeed together or all fail together; and saved evidence that remains after a restart.

The commands are ingest → propose → approve → post. Ingest records the bank message. Propose checks a suggested invoice match. Approve records a person’s decision. Post writes the journal, which is the accounting entry. Each step records a different fact, so receiving money cannot accidentally count as permission to settle an invoice.

questions.question: Is this program moving £120?
questions.answer: No. It records a payment that already arrived. The external bank transfer is outside this exercise.

questions.question: What is Chris testing beyond happy-path coding?
questions.answer: Whether the system stays correct under duplicate delivery, concurrency, stale decisions and crashes, and whether its records explain what happened.

chapters.title: The £120 story
chapters.summary: Understand the books before the database.
paragraphs: Before tenant-a receives £120 for INV-1, the customer owes that amount. The books call this debt Accounts Receivable. After payment, the Bank account is £120 higher and Accounts Receivable is £120 lower. The business has exchanged a debt for cash.

To record that exchange, the program writes two journal lines: debit Bank 12000 and credit Accounts Receivable 12000, in GBP. For these two asset accounts, a debit increases the asset and a credit decreases it. The words debit and credit do not always mean money out and money in.

A journal entry groups the accounting lines under one record. The ledger is the collection of entries. An entry balances when its debits equal its credits. Posting £120 against the wrong invoice could still balance, so balance alone cannot establish that the match is correct.

The code stores £120 as 12000 pence. These are integer minor units: whole units of the currency’s smallest denomination. Go’s int64 holds the whole number exactly within its range. The confidence score uses float64 because it is an estimate, not a monetary amount.

In the example, tenant-a has two open £120 invoices. Matching amount and currency makes each bill eligible, but cannot tell us which one the payer intended. The checks rule out invalid matches. The reviewer must still use the source evidence to judge whether INV-1 is the right match.

questions.question: Can a journal balance and still be incorrect?
questions.answer: Yes. The wrong invoice or tenant can produce equal debit and credit totals. Balance is one invariant, not the entire correctness argument.

questions.question: Why not store 120.00 as float64?
questions.answer: Binary floating-point cannot represent every decimal fraction exactly. We store 12000 integer pence so equality and sums are exact within the integer range.

chapters.title: Enough Go to read every file
chapters.summary: Read the notation without losing the business idea.
paragraphs: To follow how tenant-a’s £120 becomes an entry for INV-1, you need to read the values passed between functions. Go groups related files into packages. package recon holds the reconciliation workflow, package db opens SQLite, and package main runs the commands. A capitalised name such as Invoice is available to other packages. A lowercase name such as payment stays within its package.

A struct groups named fields, like a form. Invoice{Currency: "GBP"} creates a value with its Currency field filled in. A field’s type says what it can hold: string is text, int64 is a whole number, bool is true or false, and []Check is a list of check results called a slice.

The program must distinguish a missing amount from a supplied zero. At the JSON input boundary, *int64 is a pointer that can hold an address or nil, meaning no value. &value gets an address; *pointer reads the value there. Optional links to database records also use pointers.

Functions can return a result and an error together. (Journal, error) means “the accounting entry, plus any failure”. nil in the error position means success. if err != nil stops the operation when an error exists. := creates and assigns a local variable; = assigns to an existing one.

func (s *Service) Post(...) defines a method called with service.Post(...). The receiver s gives it access to the database and configured functions. context.Context passes cancellation and deadlines into database calls so work can stop when its caller stops waiting.

When a database operation fails, it must release its unfinished transaction. defer schedules a call for when the function exits. A deferred tx.Rollback() discards unfinished changes, but cannot undo a successful commit. A closure is a function that uses surrounding variables; transaction callbacks use this to work with the current operation’s values.

The code passes database values through SQL placeholders written ?. This keeps a value separate from the SQL command text. Exec runs a statement without returning rows. Query returns rows to loop over. QueryRow expects one row. Scan copies columns into Go variables in the listed order. rows.Err() checks whether reading failed during the loop.

JSON tags connect incoming field names to Go fields. For example, `json:"tenant_id"` connects tenant_id to TenantID. A tag does not check whether the organisation exists or the input is valid. Parsing and business rules perform those checks.

questions.question: Why is AmountMinor a *int64 in a wire struct but int64 in BankEvent?
questions.answer: The wire form needs to detect absence. After validation guarantees presence, BankEvent can hold an ordinary integer.

questions.question: Does defer tx.Rollback() undo a successful commit?
questions.answer: No. It cleans up an unfinished transaction. Once commit succeeds, Rollback is a no-op for the committed transaction.

chapters.title: The data model, line by line
chapters.summary: These forms are the vocabulary of the whole system.
paragraphs: To explain why tenant-a’s £120 settled INV-1, the program must retain more than the final accounting entry. model.go defines the records that connect the bank message to the payment, proposed match, approval and journal. It defines their fields; other files save and load them.

These records answer different questions. An event says which bank notification arrived. A payment identifies the underlying movement of money. A proposal names the suggested invoice. An approval records agreement with that proposal’s contents. The journal records the accounting result.

A retry must not record the £120 twice, but it can add evidence that the bank sent another message. This property is called idempotency: repeating the operation does not repeat its financial effect. It does not mean every table stays unchanged. Rejected or replaced suggestions can also be evaluated again.

blocks.title: Invoice: which bill, whose bill, how much?

notes.text: Invoice groups the fields that describe a customer bill. The braces enclose the record’s fields.
Use TenantID and InvoiceID together to find the correct organisation’s bill.
Compare Currency and AmountMinor with the bank payment. Status says whether the bill can still be settled.
These constants name the allowed invoice states in Go. Separate database CHECK rules enforce the stored states.

blocks.problem: The program must identify the bill without confusing two organisations’ invoices.
blocks.example: tenant-a’s INV-1 is a GBP invoice for 12000 pence. tenant-b’s INV-1 is a different bill.

blocks.title: BankEvent: notification identity versus payment identity

notes.text: EventID identifies the bank notification. TransactionID identifies the bank movement. The other fields describe its tenant, provider, currency, amount and reference.
IngestOutcome gives the result its own named string type, so code can distinguish it from ordinary text.
Accepted creates a payment. DuplicateEvent repeats an accepted notification. DuplicateTransaction records another notification about a known payment. Conflicting contents return an error.
The result includes the payment ID so the caller can continue with the existing payment after a retry.

blocks.problem: Repeated bank messages must not turn one payment into several.
blocks.example: evt-1 and evt-2 can both describe tenant-a’s £120 transaction txn-1. Their notification IDs differ; their payment identity is the same.

blocks.title: Proposal: input versus stored decision

notes.text: The suggestion supplies tenant, transaction, invoice and confidence. It does not supply amounts; the program reads those from saved bank and invoice records.
An open proposal can be replaced or posted. Rejected records a failed suggestion. Approval is a separate record, so it does not add an approved proposal state.
ID identifies the stored proposal. Fingerprint describes its tenant, transaction, invoice and confidence, so the approval can name the contents reviewed.
PaymentID is absent if no single payment was found. Checks retain the first rule results. Supersedes points from a new valid proposal to the one it replaces.
Replayed tells the caller this response reused a result. It is not a saved proposal column.

blocks.problem: A suggested match must be recorded separately from bank facts and from approval.
blocks.example: The suggestion names tenant-a, txn-1, INV-1 and a confidence score. It cannot supply a replacement amount for the stored £120 payment.

blocks.title: Approval: a named decision about exact content

notes.text: The request names the proposal and the fingerprint reviewed, plus a simulated reviewer name. The command constructs this Go value directly, so it does not need JSON field tags.
The approval saves the proposal link, reviewed fingerprint, reviewer and time under its own ID. Replayed reports a repeat request rather than another decision.

blocks.problem: A reviewer’s decision must refer to the exact suggestion they inspected.
blocks.example: Approving proposal 7 for tenant-a’s £120 against INV-1 must not authorise different contents naming INV-2. The request carries proposal 7 and its reviewed fingerprint.

blocks.title: Journal: the accounting result and its evidence links

notes.text: The two constants name the only accounts in this exercise: Bank and Accounts Receivable.
A line stores a debit or credit for one account. Database rules require nonnegative amounts and exactly one nonzero side.
These links connect the accounting entry to the payment, invoice, proposal and approval that justify it.
Currency applies to the whole entry and Lines holds its accounting sides. Replayed means this entry was already committed.

blocks.problem: The final accounting entry must show both what changed and why.
blocks.example: The £120 entry debits Bank and credits Accounts Receivable. Its links lead back to tenant-a’s payment, INV-1, the proposal and the approval.

questions.question: Does “approved” appear as a proposal status?
questions.answer: No. The proposal remains open after approval. An approvals row records the human decision; posting or replacement then changes proposal status.

questions.question: Why does an invalid proposal sometimes have no PaymentID?
questions.answer: The suggested payment may not exist within the tenant, or the transaction ID may be ambiguous. The proposal is still stored as rejected evidence.

chapters.title: The front door: parse before trusting
chapters.summary: Correct JSON shape is different from a correct match.
paragraphs: Before tenant-a’s £120 message can enter the books, the program must understand exactly what the caller supplied. parse.go checks required fields and types before any database write. A well-formed proposal can still be wrong about INV-1; later checks compare it with stored facts.

The amount must arrive as an integer, such as 12000 for £120. The parser rejects the string "12000" and the fractional number 12000.5 instead of quietly converting them. It also rejects zero and negative amounts because outgoing payments and refunds are outside this exercise.
The currency check accepts exactly three uppercase letters. GBP passes, but so does ABC. The check establishes the format of a code, not whether an official currency registry recognises it.

The decoder rejects unknown fields and extra content after the first JSON value. This catches misspelled field names and accidentally joined requests. It does not reject every possible ambiguity: repeated recognised keys still follow Go’s JSON decoder behaviour, which uses later values. Read “strict” as these particular checks.

blocks.title: Wire forms preserve missing fields

notes.text: The expression requires three uppercase letters for the currency code. Compiling it once avoids rebuilding it for each request.
Pointer fields retain whether the caller supplied a value. nil represents a missing field or JSON null; an empty string remains a supplied string.
Confidence also uses a pointer: the program must accept a supplied zero but reject an omitted score.

blocks.problem: The program must tell an omitted field apart from a supplied value before deciding whether the request is usable.
blocks.example: A missing amount is different from amount_minor: 0. Both are invalid for the £120 payment, but confidence: 0 is a valid supplied score.

blocks.title: ParseBankEvent: validate every boundary field

notes.text: Decode into the temporary input record. If decoding fails, return a named input error before using any values.
Require each identifying text field to be present and nonempty. The small list keeps a separate error message for each field.
Reference can be empty, but its field must exist. The amount must exist before the code reads through its pointer.
Require the currency-code format and a positive integer amount. Whether that amount matches INV-1 is checked later.
Copy validated fields into BankEvent and return success. Parsing has made no database writes.

blocks.problem: A malformed bank message must not become a saved payment.
blocks.example: tenant-a’s message needs GBP and the integer 12000 for £120. A quoted amount or a missing reference field is refused before any write.

blocks.title: ParseProposal: shape, confidence and negative zero

notes.text: Read the suggestion and require nonempty tenant, transaction and invoice IDs.
Require a confidence value in the permitted range. This establishes a valid score, not permission to post.
Convert negative zero to ordinary zero before hashing. SQLite stores both as zero; preserving one representation prevents a valid proposal’s fingerprint changing after storage.
Return a well-formed suggestion. Stored records still determine whether the named match is eligible.

blocks.problem: A suggestion must name its match and supply a valid score before the program checks real records.
blocks.example: A request for tenant-a, txn-1 and INV-1 with confidence 0 is shaped correctly. That alone does not establish that the £120 match is eligible.

blocks.title: decodeStrict: one object, known fields

notes.text: Create a decoder that reads the supplied JSON bytes.
Refuse unrecognised fields so a typo cannot silently disappear.
Read the first JSON value into the input record supplied by the caller.
Read again and require end-of-file. A second value or trailing garbage makes the request invalid.
Return success only after decoding the first value and ruling out extra content.

blocks.problem: Typos and accidentally joined requests should produce an error rather than be partly ignored.
blocks.example: A request with a misspelled amount field, or a second JSON object after tenant-a’s £120 message, must be refused.

questions.question: Does valid JSON mean the proposal can post?
questions.answer: No. Parsing establishes shape. Database-backed checks establish eligibility, a person approves, and posting rechecks state.

questions.question: Why does -0 matter if it equals 0?
questions.answer: Its encoded representation can differ before storage. Fingerprinting content that changes representation across storage can break the content comparison.

chapters.title: Fingerprints: approve exactly what you saw
chapters.summary: An ID says which thing. A fingerprint says what it asserted.
paragraphs: Imagine you sign a payment slip saying “apply tenant-a’s £120 to INV-1”. Someone then changes the invoice to INV-2. Your decision about INV-1 should not authorise the changed instruction. The program faces the same problem when it records approval of a suggested match.

A proposal ID answers “which stored proposal are we discussing?” A fingerprint answers “what contents did the reviewer see?” The approval stores both. When the program later acts, it checks the fingerprint against the proposal’s contents so approval of one version cannot silently apply to different contents.

The fingerprint is a short comparison value calculated with SHA-256. The program first writes selected fields into a consistent JSON representation, then hashes those bytes. Changing indentation or JSON key order in the original request does not change this representation.

The signed slip explains why the contents matter, but this hash is not a signature. SHA-256 does not authenticate the sender or reviewer, encrypt the contents, or establish that a bank claim is true. Reviewer identity is only a supplied string in this local exercise. Authentication would require a separate control.

The program needs three definitions of sameness. The event fingerprint covers the whole notification, including its ID and reference. The payment fingerprint covers the financial facts and excludes event ID and reference, so a second notification can describe the same £120. The proposal fingerprint covers the suggested tenant, transaction, invoice and confidence. Changing INV-1 to INV-2, or changing the confidence score, changes the proposal contents that require review.

blocks.title: Three different meanings of “the same”

notes.text: Hash every BankEvent field, including EventID and Reference. A changed reference under the same notification ID must be detected.

Hash tenant, provider, transaction ID, currency and amount for payment comparison. Exclude event ID and reference so a new notification can describe the same money. Include tenant to detect misrouting.
Hash the full suggestion, including confidence. Changing the invoice or rescoring the match changes what the reviewer needs to inspect.

blocks.problem: The program must distinguish a changed notification, another report of the same payment and a changed suggestion.
blocks.example: Rewording evt-1’s reference conflicts with that event. A new evt-2 can still describe the same £120. Changing a proposal from INV-1 to INV-2 requires review of the changed contents.

blocks.title: Build a versioned SHA-256 digest

notes.text: Turn the fixed Go record into JSON with a stable field order. Original request whitespace and key order no longer matter.
These callers supply validated records containing strings and numbers. Encoding failure is treated as a programming error and panics; broader input types would need a new decision.
Add a definition label and newline before SHA-256. event.v1, payment.v1 and proposal.v1 distinguish the three kinds of comparison.
Encode the resulting 32 bytes as hexadecimal text for storage and comparison. sum[:] exposes those bytes as a slice.

blocks.problem: Comparisons must ignore harmless input formatting while keeping each definition of content distinct.
blocks.example: Two differently indented JSON requests for tenant-a’s £120 produce the same selected fields. event.v1 and payment.v1 label different comparisons before SHA-256 runs.

questions.question: Why not include EventID in the payment digest?
questions.answer: A new event ID can describe the same transaction. Including it would make equivalent financial facts appear different.

questions.question: Does knowing a proposal fingerprint prove who approved it?
questions.answer: No. It binds content. Identity must come from authentication, which this local exercise simulates with a reviewer string.

chapters.title: SQLite and the rules beneath the code
chapters.summary: The application asks politely. Constraints refuse violations.
paragraphs: If the program saves tenant-a’s £120 journal but fails before marking INV-1 settled, the books disagree with themselves. A database transaction prevents that partial result: its changes commit together or roll back together. Commit makes the group permanent; rollback discards the unfinished group.

The records must also survive a restart. SQLite keeps them in a local file and provides transactions and rules that reject conflicting records. All-or-nothing writes are called atomicity. Keeping committed records through failures is called durability. They solve different problems.

Two workers could both try to post the £120. SQLite permits one writer at a time across the database. BEGIN IMMEDIATE reserves the write position before the program reads business records, so another writer cannot change them between the check and the write. A second writer waits, then can read the first writer’s committed result; the configured timeout limits the wait.

WAL, or write-ahead logging, lets readers use a consistent view while a writer works. synchronous=FULL asks SQLite to synchronise committed writes more strongly with storage. These settings support durability, but the tests here cover a process stopping around commit, not every possible hardware or storage failure.

Database constraints are rules enforced even if application code makes a mistake. A unique payment_id in journals refuses a second entry for the same payment. That rule cannot determine whether INV-1 was the right invoice, whether a person approved it, or whether all lines balance. The service and verification commands check those facts.

The executable includes its schema and creates missing database objects with IF NOT EXISTS. Reopening an older database does not update an existing table to a changed definition. An evolving product would need versioned migrations: explicit steps that bring stored structures up to date.

blocks.title: Open the database with deliberate settings

notes.text: database/sql provides Go’s database interface. The blank import registers the SQLite driver. This driver is written in Go and does not require a C compiler.
Embed the SQL schema in the executable so initialisation does not depend on finding another file at runtime.
Enable foreign-key rules, a ten-second lock wait, write-ahead logging, full synchronisation and immediate write transactions.
Escape special filename characters so a question mark or hash sign cannot alter the connection settings.
Open the database handle and execute the schema. Close it if initialisation fails. Executing the schema establishes a working connection; sql.Open alone does not.

blocks.problem: The stored £120 result needs database settings that support safe writes and useful reads.
blocks.example: When two commands try to post tenant-a’s payment to INV-1, one reserves the write transaction and the other waits up to the configured limit.

blocks.title: Invoice and payment identity

notes.text: Identify an invoice by tenant plus invoice ID. CHECK rules require a positive amount and allowed status. STRICT asks SQLite to enforce column types more closely.
The provider and transaction ID uniquely identify a payment across tenants. Changing the tenant cannot create a second copy of the same provider transaction.
This index speeds up finding payments for a tenant and transaction. It does not establish the caller’s identity or permissions.

blocks.problem: The same bill or bank transaction must not become a second business record by mistake.
blocks.example: tenant-a and tenant-b can each own INV-1. A provider’s txn-1, however, cannot become two payment records merely by changing the tenant.

blocks.title: Events and deliveries are different evidence

notes.text: Store accepted notifications separately, each linked to its payment. A provider cannot reuse an accepted event ID for another event row.
Keep well-formed delivery attempts, including duplicates and conflicts. A payment link may be absent, which avoids exposing another tenant’s payment through conflicting input.

blocks.problem: Investigators need to distinguish accepted bank facts from every delivery attempt.
blocks.example: A repeated evt-1 for tenant-a’s £120 adds delivery evidence while retaining one accepted event and one payment. A conflict is evidence too.

blocks.title: One live suggestion and one recorded approval

notes.text: Keep the suggested contents, check results, state and available links. Even a rejected suggestion helps explain what the program refused.
Allow only one open proposal in the indexed slot. The index excludes rejected, posted and replaced proposals so their history can remain.
Store one approval per proposal with the fingerprint reviewed. The unique proposal_id means a second call cannot overwrite the first decision.

blocks.problem: The program must avoid competing live suggestions and competing approvals for one suggestion.
blocks.example: A valid proposal for tenant-a’s £120 and INV-1 occupies the open proposal slot. Replacing it keeps history; approving it records one decision about its fingerprint.

blocks.title: At most one journal for each payment

notes.text: Link the journal to its supporting records. Unique payment, proposal and approval IDs prevent reusing each in a second journal. The invoice link must name an existing tenant/invoice pair.
Require a known account and exactly one positive side per line. These row rules do not total all journal lines; the service and verify command check the entry’s balance.

blocks.problem: A retry must not record the £120 twice, and each accounting line must have a valid side.
blocks.example: A second journal for tenant-a’s payment is refused. The first has a Bank debit of 12000 and an Accounts Receivable credit of 12000.

blocks.title: History cannot silently be rewritten

notes.text: Reject updates and deletions of evidence with database triggers, which run before those operations. An administrator able to remove the triggers can bypass this protection.
Permit an invoice to change only from open to settled while keeping its other fields unchanged. Refuse deletion.
Refuse proposal deletion. The full update rule permits only open to superseded or posted and protects the suggested contents from editing.

blocks.problem: Saved evidence must not be quietly edited to tell a different story.
blocks.example: After the £120 posts to INV-1, ordinary writes cannot rewrite the approval or journal. INV-1 may move from open to settled, but its amount cannot be changed through that update.

questions.question: Would a unique payment constraint make any balanced journal correct?
questions.answer: No. It prevents repetition. Matching, approval and account correctness need additional checks.

questions.question: What happens if two unrelated payments post together?
questions.answer: On SQLite they still compete for one database write lock. This is safe but limits throughput. A larger database design can lock the relevant business rows instead.

chapters.title: The transaction wrapper and honest errors
chapters.summary: Some refusals must save evidence while returning failure.
paragraphs: If a bank message contradicts tenant-a’s stored £120 payment, the caller should receive a refusal and the investigator should still see why it was refused. Returning an error and discarding every write would lose that evidence. The transaction wrapper distinguishes a saved refusal from an unexpected database failure.

Expected refusals carry a kind and a stable reason, such as invalid input, conflicting facts, a rejected action or a missing record. Callers can use those fields instead of guessing from the human-readable message. An unexpected SQL failure follows the ordinary rollback path.

keepEvidence tells the wrapper to commit the refusal’s evidence and then return the refusal error. It is safe only while every such refusal occurs before accounting writes. Using it after creating part of the £120 journal could preserve an incomplete financial operation.

Reading a trace or checking stored records needs a consistent view too. The read-only helper opens a transaction for those reads and closes it with rollback. There are no writes for it to commit. The nearby helpers provide timestamps, validate fixture invoices and describe allowed conflict details.

blocks.title: Errors are structured outcomes

notes.text: Classify expected failures into four kinds. A refused business action is different from an unexpected SQL failure.
Keep machine-readable Kind and Reason alongside a human explanation and any failed checks. Error() lets this record serve as a Go error.
Use errors.As to find a business error even through an error wrapper. IsKind and Reason expose its classification to callers.
These constructors create consistent expected errors without repeating the record-building code.
Wrap a refusal to tell the transaction helper to save its evidence. The refusal still returns as an error, not a successful action.

blocks.problem: Callers need to tell a business refusal from a broken database operation.
blocks.example: A proposal for tenant-a’s £120 against a missing INV-1 returns a named business reason. An SQL failure means the program could not complete its work.

blocks.title: inTx: follow every return path

notes.text: Start the transaction using the database’s immediate-lock setting. If that fails, do not run the business operation.
Schedule rollback before calling the business function. Cleanup also runs if that function panics.
Return immediately on an ordinary error so rollback discards unfinished writes. Only the explicit keepEvidence wrapper permits committing a refusal.
Attempt commit and report any commit failure to the caller. A retry checks saved identities rather than assuming the failed response means nothing was stored.
After commit, return either the saved refusal or success. The caller can receive an error even though refusal evidence was saved.

blocks.problem: The service must save refusal evidence without accidentally saving half an accounting entry.
blocks.example: A conflicting £120 message can leave a delivery record and return an error. An unexpected failure during posting must roll back the unfinished journal for INV-1.

blocks.title: Read snapshots, timestamps and fixture rules

notes.text: Open a read-only transaction for a consistent view, run the reader and close the transaction with rollback.
Read the configured clock and format UTC time. Tests can supply a fixed clock to produce predictable timestamps.
Require complete, positive, open fixture invoices. Settled status should come from posting, with evidence of how settlement happened.
List the fields changed in a same-tenant conflict. Cross-tenant refusal paths must avoid this detailed explanation.

blocks.problem: Inspection needs a consistent view, while fixture loading must not manufacture already-settled invoices.
blocks.example: A trace of tenant-a’s £120 reads one database view. INV-1 starts open in the fixture; posting should produce its settled state and supporting journal.

questions.question: Does returning an error always mean nothing was saved?
questions.answer: No. A domain refusal can commit its audit evidence. It must still leave the ledger unchanged. Unexpected failures roll back the transaction.

questions.question: What change would make keepEvidence dangerous?
questions.answer: Returning it after ledger writes. It instructs the wrapper to commit, so all refusal branches must remain before financial mutation.

chapters.title: Ingest: one payment, many messages
chapters.summary: Trace the first real workflow from bytes to durable identity.
paragraphs: The bank may send evt-1 twice for tenant-a’s £120 transaction txn-1. It may also send evt-2 about the same transaction. The program needs one payment record, while retaining evidence of each well-formed delivery. Ingest first parses the message, computes the event and payment fingerprints, and then checks saved records inside a transaction.

The event check asks whether this provider has used the event ID before. It reads the earliest delivery, even if that delivery was refused. Different contents under that ID conflict. Identical contents replay as a duplicate only if the earlier delivery was accepted. An identical refused message is checked again rather than treated as accepted.

For a new event ID, the payment check asks whether this provider’s transaction ID already exists. Matching financial facts mean a new notification about the existing £120 payment. Changed financial facts mean a conflict. If both identities are new, the program creates the payment, accepted event and delivery evidence together.

A conflicting payload may claim another tenant’s transaction. The program detects that routing problem but returns a generic error and keeps its delivery unlinked to the other tenant’s payment. An ordinary same-tenant conflict may include the changed fields in its explanation.

The saved database is the authority across restarts; the service does not rely on an in-memory payment cache. Retries can create delivery evidence, but do not create a second payment or journal. Malformed JSON fails before this delivery-recording path and is not retained there.

blocks.title: The service has dependencies, not hidden financial state

notes.text: Allow tests to supply a clock and a function that stops execution after posting commits. This tests saved success followed by a lost response.
Keep the database and configured functions in Service. Default to time.Now when no test clock is supplied.
Load fixture invoices together in one transaction. Identical existing invoices need no write; conflicting contents fail and ordinary failure rolls back the batch.

blocks.problem: The workflow needs a database and predictable test controls, without holding payment facts only in memory.
blocks.example: The database retains tenant-a’s £120 across restarts. Tests can supply a clock or stop the process after committing its journal for INV-1.

blocks.title: Parse and check the event identity

notes.text: Parse before opening the write transaction. Calculate separate notification and payment comparisons from the validated input.
Use the local deliver function to save this attempt’s outcome and optional payment link in the same transaction.
Read the first delivery for this event ID, including refusals. Reusing even a refused ID for changed contents must conflict.
For another tenant’s event, save an unlinked conflict and return a generic explanation. Do not reveal that tenant’s stored facts.
For a conflict within the same tenant, explain the changed fields and retain the payment link when appropriate.
Return DuplicateEvent only for matching contents previously accepted. Matching refused contents continue to the payment check rather than gaining acceptance by repetition.

blocks.problem: Reusing a notification ID must not hide a changed claim about the payment.
blocks.example: evt-1 first describes tenant-a’s £120 with reference INV-1. Repeating it unchanged is a duplicate; changing its reference to INV-2 conflicts under the same event ID.

blocks.title: Check the transaction identity, then create only if new

notes.text: Find the provider’s transaction. If the financial facts match, add the new accepted event and return the existing payment as DuplicateTransaction.
Refuse changed financial facts. Keep other tenants’ conflicts generic and unlinked; same-tenant differences can be explained.
Create a new payment only when neither identity exists. Save its event and delivery in the same transaction so an ordinary write failure discards the whole group.

blocks.problem: A new notification must not become a second copy of an existing payment.
blocks.example: evt-2 can describe txn-1’s same £120 and link to the existing payment. If it claims £125 instead, the saved financial facts conflict.

blocks.title: Identity queries and evidence insertion

notes.text: Allow a saved delivery to have no payment link. Remember whether the original outcome accepted the event so receipt alone cannot imply acceptance.
Find the earliest delivery for provider and event ID using the supporting index. Distinguish no record from a database query failure.
Decode the validated saved payload and restore its optional payment link and outcome. Accepted contents without a payment indicate inconsistent stored data.
Search across tenants internally to detect the same provider transaction being routed twice. Do not expose the other tenant’s facts in the resulting error.
For a proposal, search only its tenant and return all providers using the transaction ID. More than one candidate must be treated as ambiguous.
Write through the caller’s transaction using SQL parameters. Keep accepted event identities separate from the history of all well-formed delivery attempts.

blocks.problem: The lookup and insertion helpers must preserve identity and the evidence behind each decision.
blocks.example: Finding txn-1 across tenants can detect misrouting. Finding it for tenant-a’s INV-1 proposal must return only tenant-a’s possible payments, including ambiguity across providers.

questions.question: What is the result of evt-2 describing the same txn-1?
questions.answer: One new bank_events row and a delivery row, linked to the existing payment. Outcome duplicate_transaction; no second payment.

questions.question: Why is findPayment allowed to look across tenants?
questions.answer: It detects a provider transaction being routed to two tenants. It is internal; cross-tenant results must only produce generic errors and unlinked delivery evidence.

chapters.title: Deterministic checks: eligibility, not intuition
chapters.summary: The model supplies a suggestion. Stored facts decide whether it is allowed.
paragraphs: A suggestion says to apply tenant-a’s £120 transaction txn-1 to INV-1. Before asking anyone to approve it, the program must establish that both records exist, the payment is unambiguous and unposted, the invoice is open, and their amounts and currencies match. These are deterministic checks: the same facts produce the same results.

evaluateChecks receives those facts and returns named pass/fail results. It does not query or change the database. The caller loads the facts inside the transaction that will act on them, so another writer cannot change them between the check and the action.

The amount and currency come from the stored payment and invoice, not from the suggestion. Confidence is not a rule. A suggestion with confidence 0.99 still fails if INV-1 is for £125. A score of 0.05 can pass these rules and still need the reviewer’s judgement.

If INV-1 is missing, the program fails the invoice-exists check. It skips amount and currency comparisons that cannot be made without the record. Skipping those dependent comparisons does not turn the whole result into a pass: allPassed sees the missing-record failure.

Payment and invoice lookups stay within the proposal’s tenant. A bill belonging to tenant-b therefore appears missing to tenant-a’s match. This controls which records a match can use. It does not authenticate the caller; a production server would need to establish which organisation the caller is authorised to act for.

blocks.title: Check results and the facts they may inspect

notes.text: Give each result a stable rule name, pass/fail value and explanation. Save these first results with the proposal for later inspection.
Name the requirements explicitly: payment existence, a single candidate, no prior journal, invoice existence, open status, matching currency and full amount.
Group the inputs needed by the rules. A list of payments lets the evaluator distinguish missing, unique and ambiguous candidates.

blocks.problem: A reviewer needs named reasons why the suggested match is eligible or refused.
blocks.example: The £120 proposal for tenant-a’s INV-1 stores results such as invoice_open and amount_matches_in_full, with explanations.

blocks.title: Read the evaluator from top to bottom

notes.text: Prepare the result list and a small local function that appends a named result with its explanation.
Fail when there is no payment. Accept one candidate as unambiguous. If several providers use the ID, report ambiguity rather than choosing one.
Check for a previous journal only when there is one identifiable payment to inspect.
Require an invoice record and, when present, require it to remain open.
Compare the stored currency and integer amount when both records are available. Never use the confidence score to decide eligibility.

blocks.problem: The rules must refuse missing, ambiguous or already-used payments before comparing the proposed bill.
blocks.example: One unposted £120 payment and an open GBP INV-1 for 12000 pass the comparisons. Two providers sharing txn-1 make the suggestion ambiguous.

blocks.title: Aggregate outcomes without hiding individual failures

notes.text: Refuse the whole match if any rule fails or the result list is empty. An absent list must not silently permit the action.
Collect failed results for the error response. The proposal still retains the complete initial results, including passes.

blocks.problem: One failed requirement must prevent the whole match from passing without losing its explanation.
blocks.example: If tenant-a’s INV-1 is missing, the proposal fails even though the program cannot run the amount comparison. The error can name that missing-invoice failure.

blocks.title: Load fresh facts in the caller’s transaction

notes.text: Load facts and run the rules again. Return business refusal separately from a database failure so callers can handle each correctly.
Find candidates inside the proposal’s tenant. Check for a journal only if exactly one payment was found.
Load the invoice inside that same tenant and return the facts assembled in the transaction.
Extract the stored proposal’s suggested fields for fresh checks and content comparison.

blocks.problem: Approval and posting must use current facts rather than trusting an earlier successful check.
blocks.example: INV-1 may have been open when tenant-a’s £120 proposal was created. If another payment settles it first, a fresh check must refuse the stale match.

questions.question: Would confidence 0.05 fail these rules?
questions.answer: No. A low-confidence suggestion can pass deterministic checks and still need a person’s judgement. A high-confidence mismatch fails.

questions.question: Why repeat checks after proposal creation?
questions.answer: The world may change. Another payment might settle the invoice before approval or posting. The final decision must use current facts.

chapters.title: Keep the old suggestion when the proposed match changes
chapters.summary: A rejected suggestion should explain the failure. A replacement should show exactly what it replaced.
paragraphs: Suppose tenant-a receives £120 and the first suggestion selects INV-1. A reviewer approves that suggestion. A later suggestion selects INV-2 instead. Editing the first record would make its approval appear to cover a choice the reviewer never saw. Propose therefore saves a new record and marks the earlier open proposal as superseded, meaning replaced.

The replacement must pass all the fixed checks before it can close the earlier proposal. A suggestion for an invoice in the wrong currency is saved as rejected and leaves the valid INV-1 proposal open. Propose records a possible match; it never creates accounting entries.

An identical open or posted proposal returns the existing record with Replayed set. Replayed means the operation found a result already stored for this content. It does not mean the invoice is still eligible for a new posting. Approve and Post make their own current-state checks.

An identical rejected or superseded proposal is evaluated again. If the first suggestion arrived before the £120 payment, receipt of that payment may make the same suggestion valid later. The rejected record remains as evidence of the earlier failure.

Replacing a proposal leaves its old approval in history. That approval still names the old proposal and its fingerprint, the content digest. Because the old proposal is no longer open, Post refuses to use it. The new suggestion needs its own approval.

blocks.title: Parse, fingerprint and recognise a live replay

notes.text: An unreadable suggestion cannot be checked. Parse it first, then calculate its content digest and the time of this attempt.
Prevent a retry from creating another live version. Within the transaction, look for the same fingerprint among open or posted proposals and return that record as a replay.
If there is no existing live result, load the payment and invoice as they exist now. Earlier rejected history does not decide this attempt.

blocks.problem: Avoid another live record for the same suggestion.
blocks.example: Submitting the same tenant-a £120-to-INV-1 suggestion twice should return its existing open proposal.

blocks.title: Default to rejection; open only after all rules pass

notes.text: Retain both the attempted choice and the reason it passed or failed. Build the record from current facts and start its status at rejected.
Attach payment evidence only when the lookup found exactly one payment. Another check may still fail, so a linked proposal is not necessarily valid.
Only a proposal whose checks all pass becomes open and looks for an earlier open proposal on this payment.
Keep the earlier choice in history but prevent its approval from posting. Mark it superseded and link the replacement to it within this same transaction.

blocks.problem: Keep a valid current choice until its replacement has passed the rules.
blocks.example: An invalid INV-2 suggestion must not cancel tenant-a’s valid £120 match to INV-1.

blocks.title: Store the result even when the answer is no

notes.text: Give the saved attempt its own ID, then return that identified record to the caller.
A failed match needs durable evidence. keepEvidence tells the transaction wrapper to commit the rejected record while still returning the checks_failed error.
A passing suggestion commits as open. Both outcomes finish here without creating journal lines.

blocks.problem: Explain a refused suggestion without creating an accounting effect.
blocks.example: If INV-1 is not yet eligible for tenant-a’s £120 payment, save the failed checks so the operator can inspect them.

blocks.title: The storage rules behind replacement

notes.text: The database lookup limits replay to open or posted proposals. Rejected and superseded records do not prevent a fresh evaluation.
Find the one open suggestion for a payment. The partial unique index enforces that limit in storage as well as in this query.
Preserve the initial check results as JSON alongside the proposal’s fields. That records why this version was accepted or refused.
Change a status only if it still has the expected old value. Requiring one affected row turns an unexpected state into an error.

blocks.problem: Make replay and replacement follow the same stored rules.
blocks.example: An old rejected £120-to-INV-1 suggestion may pass later; an identical open suggestion should reuse its record.

questions.question: Can an invalid replacement invalidate a good open proposal?
questions.answer: No. If tenant-a has a valid £120 proposal for INV-1, a failed INV-2 suggestion is saved as rejected. Only a replacement whose checks all pass supersedes the open proposal.

questions.question: Why not just edit invoice_id on the old proposal?
questions.answer: The reviewer approved the old content. Editing it would blur which invoice that approval covered. A separate replacement record preserves both choices, and its supersedes link names the earlier one.

chapters.title: Approve the exact suggestion the reviewer saw
chapters.summary: A content fingerprint identifies a version. It does not establish who approved it.
paragraphs: Suppose a reviewer has inspected tenant-a’s £120 payment and selected INV-1. The approval request sends the proposal ID and the fingerprint shown with it. Comparing that fingerprint with the stored value prevents the request from approving different content by mistake.

A fingerprint is a digest calculated from the proposal fields. It is not a password, a signature from a person, or proof that anyone read the evidence. A caller who knows the fields can supply it. It binds this decision to content; it does not authenticate the reviewer or prove the invoice is correct.

This exercise accepts a reviewer name from the caller. It rejects the reserved name system, but someone can still type another name. A real service must get the reviewer’s identity from a verified sign-in and check whether that person may approve for tenant-a.

Before creating or replaying an approval for an open proposal, Approve checks the current payment and invoice again. If another payment has already settled INV-1, the old decision is no longer usable and the request is refused. If INV-2 replaced the proposal, the old proposal is refused because it is no longer open.

A proposal that has already posted has a narrow exception: an existing approval may be returned during recovery. Its invoice is expected to be settled. Repeating approval does not overwrite the original reviewer. An attempt by another reviewer returns the first approval and records the additional attempt.

blocks.title: Validate the approval request

notes.text: Ignore accidental surrounding spaces so a reviewer name is stored consistently.
Refuse a missing ID, fingerprint or name, and reserve system for automated actions. These input failures occur before any transaction or audit record; they do not verify a person’s identity.
Use one time and one proposal subject for the decision’s audit records.

blocks.problem: Require enough information to identify the reviewed decision.
blocks.example: The caller sends tenant-a’s £120-to-INV-1 proposal ID, its displayed fingerprint and a reviewer name.

blocks.title: Load the proposal and compare what was reviewed

notes.text: When a business check refuses approval, record approval_refused and preserve that evidence through keepEvidence. An audit-write failure instead returns an ordinary error.
Load the named proposal before making a decision. A database error and a proposal that does not exist have different return paths.
Compare the supplied digest with the stored one. Equality identifies the content version; it does not prove who sent the request or whether the invoice choice is right.

blocks.problem: Stop approval when the supplied version differs from the stored choice.
blocks.example: A reviewer who inspected INV-1 must not accidentally approve another proposal version by sending the wrong fingerprint.

blocks.title: Replay a decision, or make a new one after fresh checks

notes.text: Find any earlier approval, but keep checking before returning it. Existence alone does not make an unposted decision usable.
Require the proposal to remain open. Allow an existing approval on a posted proposal only so recovery can return completed history.
Recheck current payment and invoice facts for every open proposal. A now-settled invoice must cause refusal before any approval is replayed.
After the guards pass, return the first approval. If a different reviewer tried, retain the original decision and record the additional attempt.
If no earlier approval exists, save a decision naming this exact proposal and digest. Save its approved audit event in the same transaction.

blocks.problem: Do not report an old decision as usable after circumstances change.
blocks.example: If another payment settles INV-1 after tenant-a’s £120 proposal was approved, repeating approval must fail rather than report success.

questions.question: Does repeating Approve on a superseded proposal create fresh authority?
questions.answer: No. Superseded means replaced, so Approve refuses the request and records the refusal even if an old approval exists. Returning an existing approval for an already posted proposal is a separate recovery case. Post also checks stale approvals independently.

questions.question: What replaces -reviewer in production?
questions.answer: Use the identity from a verified server-side sign-in and check that person’s permissions for the tenant. A caller must not gain authority merely by sending a chosen reviewer name.

chapters.title: Post the approved £120 once, with all its related changes
chapters.summary: One transaction must save the journal, settle the invoice and finish the proposal together.
paragraphs: Tenant-a has approved matching the £120 payment to INV-1. Posting must now save two accounting lines, mark INV-1 settled and mark the proposal posted. If only some of those changes survived a failure, the database would disagree with itself. Post puts them in one transaction, so they become durable together or are rolled back together.

Post accepts an approval ID. It does not accept a model score or caller-written journal lines. It first loads the approval, then looks for a journal already created from it. If the £120 was posted before a lost response, Post returns that journal as a replay.

That completed-result lookup comes before checking whether the proposal is open. A successful posting already changed it to posted. Checking open status first would incorrectly reject the retry of a completed operation. A superseded proposal without a completed journal is different: its old approval cannot start a new posting.

For a new posting, Post checks the approval’s content fingerprint, the open proposal status and the current payment and invoice facts inside the same transaction. These checks establish whether the selected invoice can still be settled. They cannot tell whether INV-1 is the intended invoice when another equally eligible £120 invoice exists. The reviewed match still matters.

Post builds a £120 debit to Bank and a £120 credit to Accounts Receivable from the stored payment. The amounts are 12000 minor units, meaning pence for GBP. It checks that the lines balance, inserts the journal, settles the invoice and records the result. A write failure rolls all of those changes back.

The simulated crash runs after commit, when the database has already saved the result. The caller can therefore see an error even though posting succeeded. Retrying the same approval resolves that uncertainty by returning the existing journal. The retry must not create a fresh financial effect.

blocks.title: Require approval and find an already completed result first

notes.text: A posting needs a real approval ID. Reject an absent one before preparing the audit subject.
Run posting in one write transaction. Its refusal helper records the failed attempt and preserves that evidence without starting journal writes.
Load the recorded approval. A guessed or missing approval ID cannot supply authority to post.
Look up a journal by this approval before checking live proposal state. An existing result is returned with Replayed set, preventing another journal.

blocks.problem: Recover a completed posting before attempting a new one.
blocks.example: Tenant-a’s £120 was committed against INV-1, but the response was lost. The same approval must return the original journal.

blocks.title: Validate exact content, live status and current source facts

notes.text: Follow the approval’s proposal link. A missing linked record is an internal consistency error, rather than an ordinary ineligible match.
Compare the approval’s digest with the proposal’s stored digest, then recalculate the digest from the saved fields. Both the link and the content must agree.
An approval of a replaced or otherwise closed proposal cannot start a posting. Require open status before proceeding.
Reload and check the current payment and invoice within this transaction. If another payment settled INV-1, refuse before any financial write.
Take the payment and tenant from the checked source facts. The caller supplies an approval ID, not the amount to book.

blocks.problem: Make sure this approval still covers an eligible, unchanged proposal.
blocks.example: If INV-2 replaced the approved INV-1 suggestion, tenant-a’s old approval must not settle either invoice.

blocks.title: Construct and commit the accounting effect

notes.text: Build the header from checked records and retain its proposal and approval links. Debit Bank 12000 and credit Accounts Receivable 12000 for the £120 payment.
Before inserting, verify the constructed lines have equal positive totals. This checks the accounting result the function just built.
Insert the journal and lines, settle the open invoice and change the proposal to posted. Any ordinary error causes the surrounding transaction to roll back all these writes.
Add the posted audit event before the transaction wrapper commits. The returned journal ID and the audit record refer to the same result.
After a successful commit, run the simulated-crash hook only for a new posting. A hook error cannot undo saved writes; a retry returns the existing journal.

blocks.problem: Save all parts of the financial result together.
blocks.example: Posting tenant-a’s £120 to INV-1 needs matching accounting lines, a settled invoice and a completed proposal.

blocks.title: Balance, insert and settle with guarded writes

notes.text: Add the integer debit and credit amounts separately. Using minor units avoids rounding a £120 amount through floating-point arithmetic.
Require at least two lines and equal positive totals. This helper does not check tenant ownership, invoice choice or the full set of account rules.

blocks.problem: Catch a malformed set of accounting totals before storage.
blocks.example: A £120 bank debit paired with a £119 receivables credit must fail the balance check.

blocks.title: All SQL writes share the posting transaction

notes.text: Insert the journal header and obtain its ID within the supplied transaction. This function does not commit it independently.
Use that ID for each journal line. A line error returns to the caller, whose transaction rolls back the header and any earlier lines.
Settle only the requested tenant’s open invoice. Require exactly one changed row so an already-closed or missing invoice cannot look like a successful settlement.

blocks.problem: Keep storage helpers inside the caller’s all-or-nothing posting.
blocks.example: If settling INV-1 fails after tenant-a’s £120 journal is inserted, no partial journal may remain.

questions.question: Why check replay before proposal status?
questions.answer: A completed £120 posting already marked its proposal posted. Find and return that journal first. Otherwise a retry after a lost response would fail because the proposal is no longer open.

questions.question: What happens if settling the invoice fails after the journal insert?
questions.answer: The error causes the transaction wrapper to roll back. Its journal header, lines and other writes do not become a saved partial result.

questions.question: What if the crash hook returns an error?
questions.answer: The journal and settlement are already committed. Retry the same approval ID to retrieve that journal; do not treat the missing response as proof that posting never happened.

chapters.title: Explain a payment, then check that the records agree
chapters.summary: Trace follows one payment’s history. VerifyLedger checks specific rules across the stored ledger.
paragraphs: After tenant-a’s £120 payment settles INV-1, an operator needs two answers: why did we post this match, and do the stored accounting records agree? Trace answers the first by collecting the payment’s deliveries, suggestions, approvals, journal and related audit records. VerifyLedger answers the second with separate database queries.

Trace also returns rejected suggestions that could not be linked to a payment. A suggestion that arrived before the £120 event can therefore remain visible. The query uses the requested tenant and transaction rather than searching across tenants. Its output groups records by type; it is not one combined time-ordered list.

VerifyLedger checks rules such as equal debit and credit totals, the expected account directions, matching amounts and currencies, and agreement between the journal and the exact approved proposal. If the approval names INV-1 but a journal names an equal-value INV-2, balance alone would pass. The relationship check must report the mismatch.

These checks find inconsistent records. They cannot prove the original invoice choice was correct if the reviewer approved the wrong but equally eligible £120 invoice. They also do not detect every conceivable form of database damage. An empty problems list means the checks implemented here found no violation.

The database prevents ordinary updates and deletes to evidence through triggers. An administrator who can remove those triggers or replace the database file can still alter history. Reliable audit storage also needs access controls, backups and a retention policy.

Cross-tenant conflict deliveries have a known visibility gap: they are left unlinked to avoid exposing another tenant’s payment, so ordinary tenant traces cannot find them. A production design needs a separately recorded, authenticated sending tenant and a safe way for that tenant to inspect its refused attempts.

blocks.title: Trace: tenant-scoped snapshot and unresolved suggestions

notes.text: Keep payment histories and unresolved proposals in separate output fields. An attempt need not have a payment link to appear in the result.
Use one read snapshot and load only payments for the requested tenant. Then collect the evidence linked to each payment.
Also look for unlinked suggestions with the requested tenant and transaction. Report not_found only if neither payment nor unresolved evidence exists.

blocks.problem: Find the history even when a suggestion could not identify a payment.
blocks.example: Tenant-a suggests matching £120 to INV-1 before its bank message arrives. The rejected suggestion should still be traceable.

blocks.title: Build one payment’s evidence chain

notes.text: Start from the payment already selected within the tenant scope. Its identity and financial facts anchor the rest of the explanation.
Include each linked delivery in ID order and retain the raw JSON. Check both row-read and iteration errors so an incomplete read does not look complete.
Attach the proposals and their approvals. Use their internal IDs to select related audit subjects rather than unrelated decisions.
Add the journal if one exists and collect associated audit records. These grouped arrays explain the links; they do not provide a single global timeline.

blocks.problem: Follow the stored links that explain one settlement.
blocks.example: To explain tenant-a’s £120 posting to INV-1, connect its arrival attempts, proposal, approval and journal.

blocks.title: Verify the stored result independently

notes.text: Return counts and specific problems. No reported problems means these implemented checks passed, not that every possible corruption was ruled out.
Read counts and rule violations from the same snapshot so concurrent writes cannot make different checks observe different moments.
Check equal totals, the expected Bank debit and receivables credit, and matching amounts, currencies and tenants. Balance is only one requirement.
Compare the journal with the exact approved proposal: payment, invoice, tenant, approval link, content digest and posted status must agree.
Check settlement both ways. A journal must point to a settled invoice, and a settled invoice must have exactly one journal.
Run the rule queries and collect the offending record IDs. These queries provide a check separate from the code that constructed the posting.

blocks.problem: Find records that disagree even though posting code might appear correct.
blocks.example: A balanced £120 journal against INV-2 must fail verification if the approval selected tenant-a’s INV-1.

questions.question: Is trace the same as verify?
questions.answer: No. Trace collects the linked history for a tenant’s transaction. VerifyLedger runs specific consistency checks across stored accounting records. Neither proves that a reviewer chose the intended invoice among equally eligible choices.

questions.question: Can an administrator rewrite this evidence?
questions.answer: An administrator with enough access can remove database triggers or replace files. The append-only rules stop ordinary application updates and deletes; they do not make the evidence tamper-proof.

chapters.title: Turn a terminal command into one service operation
chapters.summary: The command layer checks input shape, calls the service and reports JSON with an exit code.
paragraphs: To walk tenant-a’s £120 payment through the system, an operator needs commands to load invoices, ingest an event, propose INV-1, approve that proposal and post its approval. The CLI supplies that interface. The service still decides whether each operation is allowed.

main passes the command arguments into run, then exits with the code run returns. run receives input and output streams as parameters, which lets tests capture results without depending on a real terminal. Results use JSON, while exit codes let a shell distinguish success from invalid input, conflict, rejection or an internal failure.

Check arguments before opening a database. Go’s flag parser stops at the first positional argument, such as an input filename. In this snapshot, command checks reject extra arguments, including flags left after that filename, instead of silently ignoring them. Put options before FILE. A missing filename is a usage error; a named file that cannot be read fails later when input is read.

The crash option deliberately terminates the process after posting commits. A missing success response therefore does not prove that INV-1 stayed open. Restart with the same database and post the same approval ID to recover the saved journal.

Fixture instructions assume a fresh database. On a database that already has records, proposal and approval IDs can differ. Use the actual IDs and fingerprint returned by your commands. The readable example label INV-1 refers to the invoice role; when running repository fixtures, use their literal invoice IDs.

blocks.title: Entry point, flags, database and crash simulation

notes.text: Define distinct exit codes so a script can tell invalid input, conflict, rejection and internal failure from success or simulated termination.
Pass arguments without the executable name into run. Reject an empty invocation and separate the command from its options.
Parse typed flags and validate that they belong to the selected command before opening a database.
Open the requested database only after those command checks pass. Close it when run returns normally.
When requested, install a function that exits after posting commit. os.Exit skips deferred cleanup and prevents the normal success response.

blocks.problem: Turn terminal input into a checked request and a meaningful process result.
blocks.example: An operator posts tenant-a’s £120 approval and needs to distinguish success from refusal or a simulated crash.

blocks.title: Dispatch commands without duplicating business rules

notes.text: For fixture loading, read and parse CSV before asking the service to load all invoice rows together.
For ingest and propose, read JSON and delegate. A rejected proposal can still return its saved ID and check results as useful evidence.
Construct the approval request from flags, pass the approval ID to Post, and delegate trace and verify to their service methods.
Build a JSON response and choose an exit code from the returned result. A verification report containing problems must signal failure.

blocks.problem: Keep command formatting from becoming a second copy of the financial rules.
blocks.example: The post command passes tenant-a’s approval ID to Service.Post; it does not construct its own £120 journal.

blocks.title: Input helpers and terminal contracts

notes.text: List allowed flags per command so validation has an explicit contract.
Refuse unknown commands and flags that belong to another command. These checks happen before db.Open.
Require exactly one filename for load-invoices, ingest and propose, and no positional inputs for other commands. Extra trailing tokens, including flags after FILE, cause an error.
Drop empty result values on failure and translate business error categories to process exit codes.
Read stdin when the filename is a dash; otherwise read the named file. Filename-count checks already ran, but reading the file can still fail.
Parse the five invoice CSV columns and convert the amount string explicitly to an integer. The service receives typed invoice values.
Use the configured database path when present; otherwise use the local default.

blocks.problem: Reject misleading command shapes before they touch a database.
blocks.example: Putting -db after the file containing tenant-a’s £120 event must not silently send it to the default database.

questions.question: Why not put the matching rules in the CLI switch?
questions.answer: The switch translates terminal input into service calls and formats their results. Keeping the rules in Service lets tests and a future HTTP interface use the same decisions.

questions.question: Is an HTTP API required?
questions.answer: No. The brief accepts a local CLI or API. A network interface and its authentication requirements are a separate product decision.

chapters.title: Test what survived, including after failure
chapters.summary: A correct error message is not enough if the database changed incorrectly.
paragraphs: Suppose Post refuses tenant-a’s £120 match to INV-1. A test that only checks the error could pass even if the implementation inserted a journal before returning it. The tests must inspect the final journal, lines, invoice status and evidence links as well as the response.

The happy-path test checks the exact payment amount, account directions, tenant, currency and invoice. It checks that the chosen invoice settled and neighbouring invoices stayed open. A balanced £120 entry against INV-2 would still be wrong if INV-1 was approved, so checking balance alone is insufficient.

The tests use real SQLite files in temporary directories. Duplicate deliveries may add evidence, but must not create another payment or journal. Refused operations compare the ledger before and after to show that accounting records did not change.

The service concurrency test gives competing goroutines separate database connection pools. A goroutine is a concurrently running Go function. The CLI test goes further by launching separate operating-system processes. Both check the committed result after overlap. The Go race detector checks certain unsafe uses of shared memory; it does not establish database correctness by itself.

The service crash test reports a failure after commit, then reopens the same database. The CLI crash test actually exits a process after commit with code 70. The retry must return the original journal, with one settled invoice and one financial effect. Reopening matters because an in-memory record of the first request would be gone.

A useful challenge for every assertion is: what wrong implementation would still pass? One journal could contain the wrong invoice. Equal totals could use the wrong accounts. A rejection could still leave financial changes. Assertions should rule out those concrete failures.

Mutation testing deliberately changes working code to break a guarantee, then checks that a test fails. It can reveal weak tests. A historical mutation run in a README is not evidence that it was repeated now; describe only the checks actually run for the current version.

blocks.title: Happy path: exact result and unaffected neighbours

notes.text: Start with a fresh database, ingest and propose, then inspect the checks and the approval’s reviewer and fingerprint links.
Assert the posted tenant, currency, invoice and both lines. The first successful posting must report a new result rather than a replay.
Inspect invoice statuses and ledger counts. This catches an operation that posts correctly but also changes a neighbouring invoice.

blocks.problem: Prove the complete £120 outcome, including records that should not change.
blocks.example: Matching tenant-a’s payment to INV-1 must settle INV-1 while leaving unrelated invoices open.

blocks.title: Concurrent posting: force overlap and inspect outcomes

notes.text: Prepare one approval and separate database-backed services. Release their posting attempts from a shared start signal to create competition.
Collect the concurrent results and compare journal identities. Read the full test for how it starts and waits for each worker.
After every worker finishes, verify one financial effect and a consistent ledger. No panic alone would be a much weaker assertion.

blocks.problem: Check that overlapping requests share one committed result.
blocks.example: Two workers post tenant-a’s £120 approval simultaneously; both must identify the same journal.

blocks.title: Crash and restart: durable identity survives memory loss

notes.text: Inject failure after commit and assert that the caller sees it. This puts the test in the saved-result, lost-response window.
Reopen the same database and repeat the workflow using a new service. Recovery must depend on stored evidence rather than the previous service’s memory.
Assert that the returned journal is the original replay and that final counts still show one balanced posting.

blocks.problem: Recover after the client loses the response to a saved posting.
blocks.example: Tenant-a’s £120 journal for INV-1 commits, the call fails, and a new service must find that journal.

blocks.title: Changed proposal: old approval cannot follow the new suggestion

notes.text: Create and approve the first choice, then submit a changed valid suggestion. Assert that the original proposal becomes superseded.
Attempt posting with the first approval. Require refusal and compare the ledger before and after to rule out hidden financial changes.
Approve the replacement separately and post it. Assert that only the replacement invoice settles; the earlier invoice stays open. The fixture uses literal IDs inv-1 and inv-2.

blocks.problem: Prevent approval of one version from authorising its replacement.
blocks.example: After tenant-a approves the £120 match to INV-1, a valid new suggestion selects INV-2.

questions.question: Does go test -race prove no double posting?
questions.answer: No. It detects certain unsafe accesses to shared Go memory. The database concurrency tests inspect actual committed results to check that the overlapping attempts produce one financial effect.

questions.question: What should every rejected-post test inspect?
questions.answer: Inspect both the refusal and the final stored ledger. It must have no extra journal or lines, no unintended settlement and no changed financial totals. Audit evidence may grow.

chapters.title: Predict the database after each failure
chapters.summary: For every retry, distinguish a repeated request from a new financial effect.
paragraphs: Begin with tenant-a’s £120 payment, transaction txn-1, and the proposed invoice INV-1. For each drill, say what the caller receives, which evidence records are added and whether the journal or invoice changes. Then find the query, application check or database constraint that makes that outcome happen.

Place failures in time. Before a transaction begins, there are no writes from it. During a transaction, unfinished writes must not become a partial saved result. After commit, the result is already durable even if no response reaches the caller. That last case needs a lookup of the completed result, not another payment or posting.

Do not use replay as a synonym for success in every situation. A posted journal can be returned again because it already happened. A superseded proposal cannot start a posting just because it had an approval before. A refused event repeated with the same content must remain refused.

questions.question: The identical evt-1 arrives three times. What exists?
questions.answer: There is one payment and one accepted event identity, with three delivery attempts. Each repeated acceptance identifies the same payment. No journal exists until approval and posting.

questions.question: evt-2 describes txn-1 with the same amount but a different reference.
questions.answer: It is DuplicateTransaction: another event describes the same payment. Save the new accepted event and delivery linked to that payment. Reference text is excluded from the payment digest, so this change alone does not create a financial conflict.

questions.question: evt-1 is reused with amount 13000.
questions.answer: The existing event described £120, or 12000 pence. Changing it to £130 causes event_content_changed. Keep the original source and a conflict delivery; do not add a payment or change the ledger.

questions.question: A suggestion arrives before its bank event.
questions.answer: Save a rejected proposal because no payment exists yet. After ingestion, the same suggestion is evaluated again rather than replaying the old rejection as a live result. Both attempts remain in history.

questions.question: tenant-b guesses tenant-a’s transaction ID.
questions.answer: The proposal lookup includes tenant-b, so it cannot load tenant-a’s payment. The suggestion fails without using the other tenant’s financial records. This query scope does not itself authenticate the caller’s tenant claim.

questions.question: Confidence is 1.0 but the currency is wrong.
questions.answer: The currency rule fails and the proposal is rejected. A high model score does not change evaluateChecks, create approval or permit posting.

questions.question: Two workers post the same approval at the same time.
