questions.answer: One writer commits first. The other then finds that approval’s journal and returns it as a replay. The database’s UNIQUE payment_id constraint also prevents a second journal for that payment. A lock wait can time out instead of succeeding.

questions.question: The process dies after inserting the header but before commit.
questions.answer: Those writes were uncommitted. SQLite recovery prevents them from becoming a saved partial posting. A retry can perform the complete transaction.

questions.question: The process dies after commit but before reporting success.
questions.answer: The £120 journal and INV-1 settlement are already saved. Retry the same approval ID; the completed-result lookup returns the original journal.

questions.question: A new proposal selects inv-2 after inv-1 was approved.
questions.answer: If the new suggestion passes the checks, it supersedes the earlier proposal. Posting the earlier approval fails because its proposal is no longer open. The replacement needs its own approval. These lowercase IDs are the fixture values.

questions.question: A different payment settles the invoice after approval.
questions.answer: Post reloads the facts within its transaction. invoice_open fails, the refusal is recorded, and this payment adds no journal or settlement.

questions.question: A command times out waiting for the database lock.
questions.answer: The configured wait can end with an internal error. The CLI has no automatic retry loop. The caller may retry the same operation to recover safely, using the same identity or approval rather than inventing a new one.

chapters.title: Know which guarantees stop at the exercise boundary
chapters.summary: The local workflow demonstrates controlled posting. Real users require additional identity, accounting and recovery controls.
paragraphs: For tenant-a’s £120 payment, this design can stop a retry from posting twice and can require an approval for INV-1. It cannot determine that INV-1 is the intended invoice merely because its tenant, currency, amount and status pass checks. If INV-2 is equally eligible, the reviewer still needs evidence that identifies the right invoice.

SQLite makes local operation straightforward and allows only one writer at a time. That helps serialize competing settlements. Moving to PostgreSQL would require an explicit plan for concurrency. Locking one payment is insufficient if two different payments are trying to settle the same invoice; that shared invoice needs protection too.

Immutable proposals preserve what the reviewer approved. Replacement creates another row instead of rewriting the old choice. The trade-off is more history and a fresh approval when fingerprinted content changes. Because confidence is included, even changing only the score creates a different content version.

The provider and transaction ID identify a payment under the exercise’s assumptions. A real provider may guarantee uniqueness only within a bank account or connection. The database key must follow that documented scope. A tenant value supplied by a caller cannot safely redefine payment identity.

Keeping raw messages and delivery attempts explains repeated and refused requests. It can also retain personal information. Decide who may see it, how long it stays and how it is removed or archived. Evidence collection needs a deliberate privacy policy.

The exercise trusts its local operator. Caller-supplied tenant and reviewer strings are not verified identities. Database uniqueness constraints stop duplicate keys; they do not establish who is allowed to approve. Before release, derive identity from sign-in, check tenant permissions and decide whether separate people must propose and approve.

There is no supported way to reverse a posting. If the wrong invoice was settled, a real accounting workflow should add a linked reversing entry rather than edit or delete the original journal. Rules for closed accounting periods are also outside this implementation.

Sending the journal to an external accounting system creates a second place where an uncertain response can occur. An outbox is a delivery-job record saved in the same transaction as the local journal. It prevents forgetting to send, but cannot by itself prevent a remote duplicate. The destination needs a reliable retry key or a way to identify the completed result. A lookup followed by a new request can still race.

Before trusting model suggestions, use accountant-reviewed examples that include ambiguous and adversarial cases. Measure wrong matches, missed matches and reviewer effort. Run suggestions without financial effects first, often called shadow mode. Passing technical checks is not evidence that the model chose the intended invoice.

Duplicate or unauthorised financial effects, cross-tenant access, inconsistent accounting records, weak recovery evidence and unauthenticated approval would block release. Representative evaluation is also required. Passing this exercise’s tests demonstrates the tested local behaviour, not production readiness.

When explaining AI-assisted work, separate what the repository records from what you personally checked and understand. Be ready to show the failure scenario, enforcing code and observed result behind each claim.

questions.question: What would you improve first for real users?
questions.answer: Verify who is acting and whether they may act for the tenant. Add controlled reversal and accounting-period rules, then migration and recovery procedures. Evaluate ambiguous invoice matches with representative reviewed examples before allowing real effects.

questions.question: Does an outbox guarantee exactly-once posting to an external API?
questions.answer: No. It saves a job to send with the local journal. Resolving a lost remote response without a duplicate still requires a reliable destination retry key or a way to identify the completed remote effect.

chapters.title: Practise until you can predict the next failure
chapters.summary: Learn the £120 story first, then connect each guarantee to code and evidence.
paragraphs: First, explain tenant-a’s £120 payment and INV-1 without opening the code. A delivery is an arrival attempt. A payment is the underlying financial event. A proposal suggests the invoice match. An approval records agreement to exact proposal content. A journal records the accounting effect. Explain why equal debit and credit totals do not prove the right invoice was chosen.

Next, read model.go, parse.go and schema.sql. For each field, name its source and who may change it. For each UNIQUE constraint, give a duplicate it rejects. Then name a rule that still belongs to application code, such as rechecking that the invoice is open. Do not assume a database key enforces the whole workflow.

Walk one fixture through Ingest, Propose, Approve and Post. Keep a small table of records before and after each command. Identify which transaction owns every write. Find the return that preserves refusal evidence and the return that rolls back an unexpected write failure.

Work the failure drills before reading their answers. Predict the resulting rows, then read the relevant test. Ask which assertion would fail if a guard disappeared. If none would fail, the test needs a stronger check of observable behaviour.

Explain Post from memory in this order: load approval; return a completed journal if present; check approved content; require an open proposal; reload current facts; build balanced lines; save journal and settlement together; commit; handle a lost response through retry. Then compare your explanation with the function.

Practise a small change using a disposable database. For example, describe an approval-expiry rule or add a mismatched-currency case. Write the expected response and final accounting state before changing code. This is a learning exercise, not an instruction to expand the submitted project.

A clear walkthrough can begin: “The £120 payment is recorded once even if its message arrives repeatedly. A suggestion selects INV-1, fixed checks test whether that choice is eligible, and a reviewer approves its exact content. Posting rechecks the current facts and saves the journal and invoice settlement together. Retrying the same approval recovers a completed posting after a lost response.”

Be ready to point to where the write lock begins, what commits, what rolls back and why a completed retry is safe. State the limits too: the fingerprint does not authenticate a person, and eligibility checks cannot choose between two equally eligible invoices.

questions.question: Can you describe the system in one sentence?
questions.answer: It records a payment once, checks a proposed invoice match, records approval of exact proposal content and saves a balanced, linked journal together with invoice settlement.

questions.question: What is the strongest sign you understand the code?
questions.answer: You can predict the saved state after a failure you have not seen before, find the enforcing check or constraint and write a behaviour test that would expose a wrong implementation.

chapters.title: Understand the concrete failures behind the review fixes
chapters.summary: Each fix closes a specific gap without changing the four-step workflow.
paragraphs: Review is easier to understand through the failure it prevents. The embedded source includes four focused improvements: remembering refused event identities, refusing stale approval retries, checking exact journal relationships and rejecting misplaced CLI arguments. The following tests show the first three. The CLI change is visible in the command chapter.

First, imagine tenant-a already has its £120 payment. A new event ID arrives with facts that conflict with that payment, so ingestion refuses it. The refusal still establishes that this event ID asserted particular content. Previously, only accepted bank events were used for the identity lookup. Reusing the refused ID with a different transaction could therefore be treated as a new event.

The lookup now reads the first recorded delivery, so the refused ID stays bound to its original content across restart. An index supports that lookup. A separate accepted flag keeps identity and outcome distinct: the same refused message remains a refusal rather than becoming an apparently successful duplicate.

Second, suppose INV-2 replaces the approved INV-1 proposal, or another payment settles INV-1. Repeating approval used to return the earlier decision before checking whether it was still usable. Post still refused the stale operation, but the approval response gave the wrong impression. Approve now checks open status and current eligibility before replaying an unposted decision. Already posted proposals retain a recovery exception for their completed history.

Third, a £120 journal can balance while naming a different invoice or payment from the approved proposal. The verifier now compares those exact relationships and also requires the journal’s invoice to be settled. The regression tests insert inconsistent journals directly to test that check independently. They do not show that normal Post ever produced such a swap.

Fourth, an operator could put a flag after FILE and Go’s parser would stop before reading it. The command could appear to succeed with that option ignored. Argument checks now run before opening the database and require exactly the expected positional inputs. Omitting a filename is a usage error; a supplied but unreadable file is a separate input-read failure.

The package comment describes the retry guarantee precisely: no duplicate financial effects. Repeated deliveries and rejected suggestions may still add evidence. A test that expects every retry to leave every table unchanged would assert the wrong contract.

The recorded review work reports tests first failing on the old behaviours, then passing after the fixes, along with race-enabled tests, vet and a compiled-CLI recovery walkthrough. Treat those as recorded verification for that review, not a claim that this teaching page reruns them. The code and tests here explain the guarantees; the production limits remain.

blocks.title: Prove a refused event keeps its identity after restart

notes.text: Start from a posted payment and repeat a new conflicting event twice. Both attempts must retain the transaction-conflict outcome.
Reopen the database so an in-memory identity cache cannot be the reason the test passes.
Try changing the refused event’s transaction and then its tenant. Both must conflict with the event’s established content, without exposing the original tenant’s facts.
Compare the final ledger with the original and inspect evidence counts: one payment, one accepted event and four refused delivery attempts.

blocks.problem: Remember a refused event ID even across restart.
blocks.example: After tenant-a’s £120 payment is posted, another event ID asserts conflicting facts and must not later become a different accepted payment.

blocks.title: Prove stale reapproval is a refusal, not a successful replay

notes.text: Arrange each cause separately: proposal replacement and competing settlement. Either can invalidate an unposted decision.
Repeat the original request and expect proposal_not_open or checks_failed. Returning a replayed approval would misreport its usability.
Check that financial records did not change and that the refused request left its own audit evidence.

blocks.problem: Refuse an approval retry that no longer represents a usable unposted choice.
blocks.example: Tenant-a approved INV-1 for £120, but INV-2 replaced that suggestion or another payment settled INV-1.

blocks.title: Test the verifier without trusting the posting function

notes.text: Define three wrong relationships independently so a failure identifies which rule is missing.
Create valid source and approval records, then insert a broken journal directly. Bypassing Post ensures the verifier must inspect invalid stored output.
Add balanced lines and the selected statuses. Matching totals and currencies deliberately remove balance as a way to catch the wrong relationship.
Require VerifyLedger to name the violated relationship. An empty problem list would show that the independent check missed this case.

blocks.problem: Test the verifier with mistakes that the posting service normally prevents.
blocks.example: A journal uses equal £120 amounts but names another invoice or payment, or leaves INV-1 open.

questions.question: Why is a rejected event still an identity fact?
questions.answer: Receipt establishes that this event ID asserted particular content. Acceptance decides whether that content may enter the payment workflow. Refusing the financial claim does not erase the fact that the ID was used.

questions.question: Why not call an identical rejected event a successful duplicate?
questions.answer: That would turn a refusal into apparent acceptance. Remember both the content identity and its outcome, so repeating the same refused message remains a refusal.

questions.question: Why can a posted proposal replay approval when an open stale one cannot?
questions.answer: The posted proposal returns a completed historical decision during recovery. An unposted decision must still be usable now. Its invoice may have been settled by another payment, whereas a posted proposal’s own settlement is the expected completed result.

questions.question: Why directly insert broken journals in verifier tests?
questions.answer: Post normally prevents those wrong results. Direct insertion gives the verifier invalid records to inspect independently, including equal-value records whose totals still balance.

questions.question: Why check CLI arguments before db.Open?
questions.answer: A malformed command should fail before opening or creating a database. In particular, a flag placed after FILE must not be silently ignored while the command performs a financial operation with different options.
